ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Hand Surgery Consultation — Leonardo da Vinci — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week review with nerve conduction studies, EMG, and nerve ultrasound; diagnosis; hand surgery consultation; start of splinting, hand therapy, and a statin

text.paragraph: Four weeks of numbness of the ulnar fingers, weakness, and clawing of the right hand after a fall onto the bent elbow in a 65-year-old left-handed artist who paints with the right hand. Stroke has been excluded by examination and MRI. Please confirm the site and severity with nerve studies and ultrasound and advise on splinting, hand therapy, and surgery. [S]
Urgency: Soon, within two weeks; motor weakness with early wasting. [S]

list.item: Do nerve conduction studies, EMG, and ultrasound confirm ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, and do they exclude a C8 radiculopathy, plexopathy, or a lesion at the wrist?
How severe is it, and is there axonal loss?
Which splints and hand therapy do you advise, and is a corticosteroid injection useful?
Should he have surgery now or after a trial of conservative treatment, and when should that decision be made?
If surgery is needed, which procedure, and what is the place of tendon transfers for the claw?
How can he keep working, with his left hand and with adapted tools?

text.paragraph: Mr. da Vinci is seen at the request of Dr. Carrow-Asante, six weeks after he fell onto his bent right elbow on stone stairs. Numbness of the little finger and inner ring finger began within two days, followed by weakness and curling of the ring and little fingers. He is left-handed for drawing and writing but uses the right hand to hold the palette and for brushwork on large panels, and he leans on his elbows for hours at a drawing table. Symptoms have not changed in two weeks of avoiding pressure on the elbow. He has had no previous elbow injury, neck pain, or symptoms in the other hand. He has no diabetes, and he does not smoke. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: A note by his grandfather Antonio records that his grandson, son of Ser Piero, was born on Saturday 15 April [1452] at the third hour of the night (Julian calendar; 24 April 1452 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar). The museums of Vinci read the note as placing his birth in Vinci itself; a long tradition places it in a farmhouse at nearby Anchiano. [D]
He was the son of Ser Piero da Vinci, a notary, and a woman named Caterina; a land-office return of 1458 lists 'Lionardo son of the said Ser Piero, not legitimate, born of him and Chaterina'. [D]

He was left-handed: the shading and hatching of his drawings slope from upper left to lower right, and his private notes, from his early twenties onward, are written in mirror script with the left hand. A review of the documents concluded that he used his right hand for work other than drawing and writing, and it has been claimed that he never painted with his left hand. [D]

The biographer Giorgio Vasari wrote that he was physically so strong that with his right hand he could bend the ring of an iron door knocker or a horseshoe as if they were lead; an engraving of about 1505 shows him playing the lira da braccio. [D]
At the invitation of King Francis I, who called him 'my father', he settled at the Château du Clos Lucé, at Amboise, in the autumn of 1516. [D]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Ulnar neuropathy at the right elbow (cubital tunnel), post-traumatic (G56.21). Moderately severe ulnar neuropathy at the elbow after a blow to the nerve at the cubital tunnel, with partial conduction block, focal demyelination, and some axonal loss (active denervation in the hand muscles). The studies meet AANEM criteria for localization at the elbow and exclude a lesion at the wrist, a C8 radiculopathy, and a lower trunk plexopathy. The nerve does not sublux, and there is no fracture, ganglion, or mass. Because the injury was acute and part of the deficit is conduction block, some recovery with protection of the nerve is likely, but the axonal loss and early wasting mean that recovery may be incomplete. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Today's nerve conduction studies: right ulnar motor conduction velocity 36 m/s across the elbow against 57 m/s in the forearm, a 38 percent fall in compound muscle action potential amplitude across the elbow, and reduced right ulnar sensory and dorsal ulnar cutaneous responses; median, radial, and left ulnar studies normal. Needle EMG: fibrillation potentials and reduced recruitment in the first dorsal interosseous and abductor digiti minimi, milder changes in the deep flexor of the little finger, normal flexor carpi ulnaris, abductor pollicis brevis, extensor indicis, and C8 paraspinal muscles. Ultrasound: ulnar nerve cross-sectional area 14 mm2 at the medial epicondyle against 7 mm2 in the forearm, no subluxation, no ganglion or mass. MRI of the brain (no infarct), X-ray of the elbow (no fracture; small medial osteophyte), and ECG (sinus rhythm) from the first visit. [S]

list.item: Conservative treatment for about three months from the injury: a night splint holding the elbow at about 45 degrees, a gel elbow pad, no leaning on the elbow, and no prolonged elbow bending. [S]

A daytime hand-based anti-claw splint for the ring and little fingers to improve grasp, and hand therapy twice a week for strength, dexterity, and adapted tools: built-up brush handles, a lighter brush, and a palette fixed to the easel. [S]
No corticosteroid injection, which the Cochrane review found no better than placebo. [S]

Review at about three months from the injury with grip, pinch, two-point discrimination, and the QuickDASH; if motor strength has not clearly improved, or if weakness or wasting progress at any time, I would advise surgery rather than waiting longer. [S]

If surgery is needed, in situ decompression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow, which the Cochrane review found as effective as transposition with fewer wound infections; anterior transposition only if the nerve subluxes at operation. Repeat nerve studies are not needed before surgery unless the picture changes. [S]
Tendon transfers to correct the claw only if it persists a year or more after decompression. [S]
He should keep drawing, writing, and teaching with his left hand without restriction, and paint with the adapted tools and help with heavy or prolonged right-hand tasks. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Carrow-Asante the same day; Mr. da Vinci agrees with the plan and was fitted with both splints in the clinic today. [S]
Follow-up: Primary care reviews him every four to six weeks. I will see him at about three months from the injury, or sooner if weakness worsens. [S]
